 Economy Petrol price stays flat, diesel cost to decrease as levy relief kicks in
 Diesel prices fall by up to R1.20 as government rolls out temporary R10bn levy relief
 November 03, 2026 3 min read 
 Share current article via Email Share current article via Facebook Share current article via Twitter Share current article via LinkedIn Stella Mapenzauswa
 Economics Editor
 Opens in new window Opens in new window Enter fullscreen mode displaying this image. Expand A motorist refuels at a Johannesburg petrol station as diesel prices drop and petrol remains steady following government levy relief. Picture: Antonio Muchave 
 Story audio is generated using AI 
 Petrol prices will remain at historical highs this month as global oil prices stay elevated, while diesel will cost up to R1.20 a litre less from Wednesday as a temporary general fuel levy cut announced in the medium-term budget cushions the impact of the US-Iran war.
 South Africa is a net importer of crude oil and finished petroleum products and has felt the effect of global oil supply constraints as the nine-month Iran-Iraq conflict has disrupted flows through the strategic Strait of Hormuz.
 Both 93-grade and 95-grade unleaded petrol will dip by just 1c a litre at the pump, but the wholesale price of diesel, which is not regulated at the retail level, falls by R1.10 for the 0.05% sulphur grade and R1.20 for the 0.005% sulphur grade, the department of mineral & petroleum resources said in a statement on Tuesday.
 Domestic fuel prices lag behind international movements by about a month, based on the cost of importing the products over the preceding 30 days, calculated by the state Central Energy Fund (CEF).
 The department said that during the period under review, the average Brent crude oil price increased from $101 to $108 a barrel due to uncertainty caused by the conflict, including attacks on Saudi Arabian infrastructure, as well as high freight and insurance costs caused by ship-to-ship transfers.
 “The average international product prices of petrol, diesel and illuminating paraffin increased during the period under review. Middle distillate prices are mainly affected by tight global supply, higher seasonal demand ahead of the winter in the northern hemisphere and the continued Russia/Ukraine conflict,” it said.
 The rand depreciated, on average, against the dollar, leading to higher contributions to the basic fuel prices of petrol, diesel and illuminating paraffin by 36.93c a litre, 49c and 49.26c, respectively.
 In his medium-term budget policy statement to parliament on October 21, finance minister Enoch Godongwana announced that the general fuel levy , one of several that are built into fuel prices, would be reduced by R3 a litre for diesel and R1.50 a litre for petrol from November 4 until December 1. Thereafter, the relief will continue at a lower amount until January 5, with the diesel levy reduced by R1.50 a litre and the petrol levy by R1 a litre.
 For this, the National Treasury has set aside R10bn, adding to the R17.2bn it forfeited in revenue through a similar measure between April and June.
 The general fuel levy reprieve will this month be diluted by an increase in the slate levy, a variable charge added to the price of petrol and diesel to recover shortfalls in the slate fund, which the government uses to refund licensed fuel importers for the financial difference between what they actually pay for fuel on global markets and the regulated price at which they have to sell it locally.
 The department of mineral & petroleum resources said the combined cumulative petrol and diesel slate balances at the end of September amounted to a negative balance of R15.88bn. 
 “In line with the provisions of the self-adjusting slate levy mechanism, a slate levy of 135.84c/ l will be implemented into the price structures of petrol and diesel. The increase on the slate levy will be from 87.66c to 135.84c, resulting in an increase of 48.18 c/ l in the price structure of petrol and diesel,” it said.
 Despite the latest general fuel levy concession, the latest fuel price adjustment still leaves the price of petrol more than 48% higher at R30.24 a litre in Gauteng than it was before the Middle East war made its impact felt, while the wholesale cost of diesel has soared over 66% to R30.86, according to CEF data.
